title: Priority leakage causing execution-path starvation during capacity surge — action items and mitigations
creator: Ava Chen
summary: A production incident during a multi-tenant capacity surge exposed a scheduler policy bug where priority metadata leaked between request classes. The leakage caused execution-path starvation for quantized attention kernels and aggressive KV-cache eviction, producing sustained P95/P99 latency regressions for a subset of hosted customers.
description: What happened: Around 2026-02-18 03:14 UTC we observed a spike in p95/p99 latency across several models served on shared pools. Initial triage showed normal GPU utilization but elevated request queue times. Investigation traced the root cause to a scheduler policy mismatch: when scheduler attempted to reassign slots during a burst, the per-request priority bitset failed to clear correctly for certain preempted sessions. As a result, lower-priority traffic temporarily inherited higher-priority placement tokens, starving execution paths that handle tiled attention and quantized kernels, and triggering repeated cold-probing into alternate kernels. Concomitant KV-cache eviction hysteresis exacerbated token-level recomputation and cache-warmup delays. Impact window lasted ~47 minutes with noticeable customer errors for real-time chat endpoints and degraded throughput for large-context generation workloads.

investigation_notes: Repro: synthetic workload that blends high QPS low-latency chat traffic with occasional long-context batches reproduced priority leakage after scheduler rebalancing under sustained burst

Root cause: priority bitset not reset in fast-path when preempting requests; race between slot reclaim and request-context recycling. This allowed tokens to persist for new allocations for up to 30s depending on garbage collection cadence.
Secondary effect: KV-cache eviction policy used a time-based TTL that interacted poorly with burst-induced kernel probing, causing repeated cache misses for rolled-over contexts.
Kernel selection thrash: quantized attention kernels were repeatedly probed and compiled causing jitter; this amplified tail latency despite nominal GPU utilization.
Scope: affected shared-hosted pools with mixed tenancy where burst isolation fence was not configured by default. Dedicated pools unaffected.
Telemetry used: per-request trace ids, kernel probe logs, KV-cache eviction traces, scheduler slot lifecycle logs, flamegraphs from runtime threads.
decisions: Roll back in-flight scheduler micro-optimizations that introduced the fast-path priority reuse (temp revert patch P-2026-02-18-01).
Introduce an explicit 'priority reset' step in the slot recycle codepath to guarantee deterministic clearing before reuse.
Add a short-lived eviction hysteresis window (2s) for KV-cache entries immediately following a kernel probe to allow cache warm-up without immediate eviction.
Throttle kernel probing during detected capacity rebalances to a configurable rate (default 5/sec per-node).
Make burst isolation fence opt-out rather than opt-in for shared pools; default to stricter isolation while we iterate.

risks_considered: Aggressive hysteresis could increase memory usage for KV-cache - trade-off: small 2s window chosen after benching (memory + latency trade-off).
Slower probe rates may delay fallback to faster kernels for some edge inputs - mitigated by selective probing only for models with >5s average context generation time.
Making burst fence default may slightly reduce aggregate throughput for mixed-tenant pools; mitigated by offering pool-level override and monitoring.
